Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor: Andrew was born second in the line of succession to the British throne and is eighth as of 2026.
In what year was Boris Yeltsin born?
Boris Yeltsin: Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin (1 February 1931 – 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.
In what year was Henry VII of England born?
Henry VII of England: Henry was the son of Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, and Lady Margaret Beaufort.
In what year did Kim Jong Il die?
Kim Jong Il: Posthumously, Kim Jong Il was declared an Eternal Leader of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK).

Charlemagne's reign was marked by political and social changes that had lasting influence on Europe throughout the Middle Ages.
In what year did Louis XVI die?
Louis XVI: The son of Louis, Dauphin of France (son and heir apparent of King Louis XV), and Maria Josepha of Saxony, Louis became the new Dauphin when his father died in 1765.
In what year was Habsburg monarchy founded?
Habsburg monarchy: It became extinct in the male line in 1740, but continued through the female line as the House of Habsburg-Lorraine.

Republican Party (United States): The Republican Party, also known as the Grand Old Party (GOP), is a right-wing to far-right political party in the United States.

Big Bang: The Big Bang is a physical theory that describes how the universe expanded from an initial state of high density and temperature.

Moodle: Martin Dougiamas. Moodle ( MOO-dəl) is a free and open-source learning management system written in PHP and distributed under the GNU General Public License.
In which country did the Battle of the Camel take place?
Battle of the Camel: Iraq. The Battle of the Camel, also known as the Battle of Basra (Arabic: معركة الجمل, romanized: Maʿrakat al-Jamal) took place in 656 CE outside of Basra in Iraq.
In which country is Republican Proposal based?
Republican Proposal: Argentina. Republican Proposal (Spanish: Propuesta Republicana), usually referred to by its abbreviation PRO, is a political party in Argentina.
In which country was the Caliphate of Córdoba?
Caliphate of Córdoba: Spain. The Emirate of Córdoba, and from 929, the Caliphate of Córdoba, was an Arab Islamic state ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 756 to 1031.
In which country was the Sultanate of Ternate?
Sultanate of Ternate: Indonesia. The Ternate kingdom was established by Momole Cico, the first leader of Ternate, with the title Baab Mashur Malamo, traditionally in 1257.
In which country is Battle of Shanghai?
Battle of Shanghai: Taiwan. It resulted in the Japanese capture of Shanghai and heavy destruction to the city.
In which country is People's Action Party based?
People's Action Party: Singapore. The PAP was established in 1954 as a conventional centre-left party.
In which country did the Kataeb Party take place?
Kataeb Party: Lebanon. The Phalangists were responsible for the Black Saturday massacre, the Tel al-Zaatar massacre, Ehden massacre, and the Karantina massacre.
In which country is Chakri dynasty?
Chakri dynasty: Thailand. The Chakri dynasty, unofficially the House of Chakri, is the current reigning dynasty of the Kingdom of Thailand.
In which country was Great Smog of London?
Great Smog of London: United Kingdom. The Great Smog was a severe air pollution event that affected London, England, in December 1952.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Sardinia?
Kingdom of Sardinia: Italian. Beginning in 1324, James and his successors conquered the island of Sardinia and established de facto their de jure authority.
Which of these was an official language of the Aztec Empire?
Aztec Empire: Classical Nahuatl. Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.
Which of these was an official language of Congo Free State?
Congo Free State: French. It was privately owned by King Leopold II, the constitutional monarch of the Kingdom of Belgium.
Which country uses the Sicilian piastra as its official currency?

The Sicilian piastra is the official currency of Kingdom of Sicily. It was a successor state of the County of Sicily, which had been founded in 1071 during the Norman conquest of the southern peninsula.
This member of the Imperial House of Japan reigned as the 125th emperor from 1989 until his abdication in 2019, with his era named the Heisei era — who is he?
Akihito (born 23 December 1933) is a member of the Imperial House of Japan who reigned as the 125th emperor of Japan from 7 January 1989 until his abdication on 30 April 2019.
This political philosophy advocates for abolishing authority and hierarchy, and is described as the libertarian wing of the socialist movement. What ideology is this?
Anarchism is a political philosophy and movement that seeks to abolish all institutions that perpetuate authority, coercion, or hierarchy, primarily targeting the state and capitalism.

Convicted as a war criminal for his role in the deportation of Dutch Jews while serving as Reichskommissar of the Netherlands, this man had briefly been Austria's chancellor before the 1938 Anschluss — who was he?

Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Austrian German; 22 July 1892 - 16 October 1946) was an Austrian Nazi politician and convicted war criminal who served as Chancellor of Austria in 1938 for two days before the Anschluss.
This 1944 amphibious assault on a Pacific island put Japan's home cities within range of B-29 bombers and triggered the resignation of Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō — which engagement?
Battle of Saipan was an amphibious assault launched by the United States against the Empire of Japan during the Pacific campaign of World War II between 15 June and 9 July 1944.
Originally a townhouse built for a duke in 1703, this London landmark was bought by George III in 1761 as a home for Queen Charlotte — what is it?
Buckingham Palace is the official residence and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom in London.
Writing mainly in Russian but also in his native tongue, this author became one of the most celebrated figures in all of Kyrgyz literature — who is he?
Chinghiz Aitmatov (12 December 1928 - 10 June 2008) was a Kyrgyz author who wrote mainly in Russian, but also in Kyrgyz.
Taking office at just 35, this Ecuadorian businessman-turned-politician became the second-youngest president in his country's history. Who is he?
Daniel Noboa (born 30 November 1987) is an Ecuadorian politician and businessman serving as the 48th and current president of Ecuador since 2023.
First held on April 22, 1970, this globally coordinated annual event rallies support for environmental protection — what is it?

Earth Day is an annual event on April 22 to demonstrate support for environmental protection. This day of nature's equipoise was later sanctioned in a proclamation written by McConnell and signed by Secretary General U Thant at the United Nations.
This political position argues the EU is too bureaucratic, insufficiently democratic, and erodes national sovereignty, with its mildest form seeking reform rather than exit — what is it called?
Euroscepticism is a political position involving criticism of the European Union (EU) and European integration.
Rising from a career as a shipowner to minister for marine and colonies, this man served as President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899 — who is he?
Félix Faure (30 January 1841 - 16 February 1899) was President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899.
Triggered by the 1929 Wall Street crash, this decade-long global economic downturn brought mass unemployment to the US, UK, and Germany — name the era?
Great Depression was a severe global economic downturn from 1929 to 1939.

Raised on a farm outside Hamilton before lecturing in politics at the University of Auckland, this Labour figure went on to lead her country for nearly a decade and later ran the UN's development programme — who is she?

Helen Clark (born 26 February 1950) is a New Zealand politician who served as the 37th prime minister of New Zealand from 1999 to 2008 and was the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme from 2009 to 2017.

Leading a party called the Free Voters since 2018, this German politician serves as Bavaria's deputy minister president and its state minister for economic affairs, regional development, and energy — who is he?

Hubert Aiwanger (born 26 January 1971) is a German politician and party leader of the Free Voters since 2018, the Deputy Minister President of Bavaria and Bavarian Minister of Economic affairs, Regional Development and Energy.
A scion of a family that owns the Hyatt hotel chain, this Democratic politician has served as the 43rd governor of Illinois since 2019 — who is he?
JB Pritzker (born January 19, 1965) is an American politician, philanthropist, and businessman serving since 2019 as the 43rd governor of Illinois.

Educated at Wheaton College in the United States, this monarch became the world's youngest reigning king at age 26 when his father abdicated the throne of a small Himalayan kingdom in 2006 — who is he?
Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck (born 21 February 1980) is the current King of Bhutan, reigning since 9 December 2006.

This South African politician founded and leads a communist, black nationalist party, having previously served as president of the African National Congress's Youth League before his expulsion from the party in 2012 — who is he?
Julius Malema (born 3 March 1981) is a South African politician.

Beginning in 1881 with the crowning of a Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen prince as King Carol I and ending with King Michael I's 1947 abdication, this constitutional monarchy grew from an earlier union of Moldavia and Wallachia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Romania was a constitutional monarchy that existed from 1881 to 1947.
Championing free speech, free assembly, market economies and the rule of law, this political philosophy centers on the rights of the individual — what is it?
Liberalism is a political and moral philosophy based on the rights of the individual, liberty, consent of the governed, political equality, right to private property, and equality before the law.
A leading Indian LGBT activist who runs the Lakshya Trust, he is the probable heir to a former Maharaja and the world's first openly gay prince — who is it?
Manvendra Singh Gohil (born 23 September 1965) is a son and probable heir of former Maharaja of Rajpipla.

Before founding Herut and Likud and becoming an Israeli prime minister, he led the militant Irgun and proclaimed a 1944 revolt against British rule, behind attacks like the King David Hotel bombing — who was he?
Menachem Begin (16 August 1913 - 9 March 1992) was an Israeli politician who founded Herut and Likud and served as prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983.
Serving as leader of the house in Madhya Pradesh's legislative assembly, this BJP politician became the state's Chief Minister — who is he?
Mohan Yadav (born 25 March 1965) is an Indian politician serving as the current Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh and also serving as leader of the house in legislative assembly.
Founded in Turkey in 2018 by the son of a former prime minister, this Islamist movement sees itself as heir to his father's 1990s movement and the Millî Görüş ideology — which one?
New Welfare Party is an Islamist and ultraconservative political party in Turkey, founded on 23 November 2018.
Sparked by allegations of massive fraud in a 2004 presidential runoff, this wave of protests centered on Kyiv brought political upheaval to Ukraine that winter — what event is it known as?
Orange Revolution was a series of protests that led to political upheaval in Ukraine from late November 2004 to January 2005.

This ancient people settled along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age, organizing their territory into a confederation of city-states with a language whose origins scholars still debate — who were they?
Philistines (LXX Koine) were an ancient people who lived along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age.
Worshipped as the seventh avatar of Vishnu and considered the ideal man, this Hindu deity is the hero of an ancient epic poem — who is he?
Rama is a major deity in Hinduism.
A leading theorist of Germany's SPD, she broke away to co-found the Spartacus League that became the KPD, and wrote influentially on imperialism and revolution — who is she?
Rosa Luxemburg (5 March 1871 - 15 January 1919) was a Polish and naturalised-German Marxist theorist and revolutionary.
In Egyptian mythology, this warrior goddess also presided over medicine, carried the epithet 'the eye of Ra' as a solar deity, and was closely linked with the goddesses Hathor and Bastet. Who is she?
Sekhmet (or Sachmis, from Ancient) is a warrior goddess as well as goddess of medicine.
Serving as the 39th US vice president before resigning in 1973 under Richard Nixon, this politician was only the second VP in history to resign — the first was John C. Calhoun in 1832 — who was he?
Spiro Agnew (November 9, 1918 - September 17, 1996) was the 39th vice president of the United States, serving from 1969 until his resignation in 1973 under President Richard Nixon.
This divine hero of Greek mythology, raised by his mother Aethra and said to be the son of either the king of Athens or the sea god Poseidon, is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus (Ancient) was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur.
This Roman goddess of love and beauty was said to be the ancestor of the Roman people through her son Aeneas, who fled the fall of Troy. Who is she?
Venus (mythology) (Classical) is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory.
A fierce opponent of slavery's spread, this Secretary of State served the Union through the Civil War and negotiated the treaty to buy Alaska. Who was he?

William H. Seward (May 16, 1801 - October 10, 1872) was an American politician who served as United States Secretary of State from 1861 to 1869 and earlier served as governor of New York and as a United States senator.
Elected in 2007 to the nine-member Politburo Standing Committee, the Chinese Communist Party's top decision-making body, this former senior leader once wielded major power in Beijing — who is he?
Zhou Yongkang (born December 3, 1942) is a former senior leader of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Allegedly the first Syrian to hold the position, this militant leader served as the fourth so-called caliph of the Islamic State from November 2022 until his death in April 2023. Who was he?
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi: Islamic State leader from 2022 to 2023.
A nephew and son-in-law of his predecessor Jalaluddin, this Delhi Sultan fended off several Mongol invasions and overhauled revenue and price-control policy from 1296 to 1316 — who was he?

Alauddin Khalji: Sultan of Delhi from 1296 to 1316. Alauddin Khalji (Persian: علاء الدین خلجی; born Ali Gurshasp; c. 1266 – 4 January 1316) was the Khalji dynasty Sultan of Delhi from 1296 until his death in 1316.
Known to local tribespeople as the 'hero of the jungle,' this Indian revolutionary led a 1922 guerrilla rebellion against British rule in the Andhra-Odisha borderlands — who is he?
Alluri Sitarama Raju: Indian freedom fighter and revolutionary.
Serving as Governor of Jakarta before running for president in 2024, this Indonesian politician founded a program that sends university graduates to teach for a year nationwide — who is he?

Falling on the tenth day of the first month of the Islamic calendar, this commemoration is marked by Sunni Muslims with voluntary fasting, recalling events like Moses parting the Red Sea and Noah leaving the Ark — what is it?
Ashura: Tenth day of the Islamic month of Muharram. Ashura is celebrated in Sunni Islam through supererogatory fasting and other acceptable expressions of joy.

Fluent in Cherokee, Choctaw, and several other Native languages, this man escaped slavery and went on to rack up over 3,000 arrests as one of the first Black deputy U.S. Marshals west of the Mississippi — who was he?

Drawing on Bolshevism and anarchism, this Indian revolutionary's largely symbolic bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly and a jail hunger strike made him a folk hero — and a martyr after his execution at age 23; who was he?
Practiced by early humans and often paired with a funeral ceremony, this method of laying the dead to rest involves placing a body into the ground or a mausoleum — what is it?
Burial: Ritual act of placing a dead person or animal into the ground.

In 1989, the assault of a young woman running through a Manhattan green space led to the conviction — and eventual exoneration — of five teenagers now known as the Exonerated Five. What is this notorious incident known as?
Central Park jogger case: 1989 crime in New York City.

A West Virginia farm boy who started WWII as an Army private and aircraft mechanic before becoming a flying ace, in October 1947 he became the first pilot confirmed to break the sound barrier in level flight — who was he?
Chuck Yeager: American flying ace and test pilot (1923–2020)

Marching his 13th Legion over a forbidden river into Italy in January 49 BC, Julius Caesar defied the Senate and triggered a civil war that made him dictator for life — this act gave its name to what idiom for a point of no return?
Crossing the Rubicon: Idiom meaning a point of no return. Caesar was not allowed to command an army within Italy proper, and by crossing the river with his forces was defying law and risking death.
Bribed by Philistine lords to learn the secret of a mighty Nazirite's strength, this biblical woman finally coaxed out the truth about his hair — who is she?
Delilah: Woman in the Book of Judges of the Hebrew Bible.
First ruled from 918 by Richard the Justiciar and later inherited by a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty, which feudal territory belonged to the medieval Kingdom of France?
Duchy of Burgundy: Vassal territory of France, 918–1482.
Centered in what is now southwestern Iran, with its capital at Susa, this Bronze Age civilization was known to classical writers as Susiana. What was this ancient Near Eastern civilization called?
Elam: Ancient pre-Iranian civilization between 3200 and 539 BC.
A five-time Socialist Party candidate for U.S. president, this labor leader co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and led a major railway strike against the CB&Q line in 1888. Who is he?
Eugene V. Debs: American labor and political leader (1855–1926)
It erupted in 1989 when Charles Taylor's NPFL invaded from Ivory Coast to topple President Samuel Doe, who was soon captured and executed by a splinter faction — which conflict is this?
First Liberian Civil War: 1989–1997 war in West Africa.
According to Galatians chapter 5, nine virtues — including love, joy, peace, and self-control — mark a life lived in step with God's presence; what biblical term describes this list?
Fruit of the Holy Spirit: Biblical term.
Meaning 'the one who yawns' in Mescalero-Chiricahua, this name belonged to the Bedonkohe Apache medicine man who led raids against Mexican and U.S. forces from 1850 to 1886. Who was he?
Geronimo: Leader of the Bedonkohe Apache (1829–1909)
One of the original Mercury Seven, this astronaut became the second American in space in 1961 and later commanded Gemini and Apollo missions — who is he?
Ruling from the mountain fortress of Alamut from 1090, this founder of the Order of Assassins was dubbed the 'Old Man of the Mountain' by Marco Polo — who was he?
Hasan-i Sabbah: Ismaili religious and military leader (c. 1050–1124)
This reclusive Afghan cleric has almost no digital footprint beyond two photographs and a few audio recordings, yet has led his country's ruling movement since 2016 — who is he?
Hibatullah Akhundzada: Supreme Leader of Afghanistan since 2021.
This grandson of Genghis, whose army sacked Baghdad in the 13th century and ended the Abbasid dynasty, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia — who was he?
Hulegu Khan: Western Asian Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265)
The first Muslim president of Guyana, this politician was sworn in during August 2020 after a lengthy recount dispute and later won a second term — who is he?
Irfaan Ali: President of Guyana since 2020. Mohamed Irfaan Ali (born 25 April 1980) is a Guyanese politician serving as the tenth and current president of Guyana since 2020.

Raised in the wealthy capital of Gurganj, this able general became the last Khwarazmshah of the Anushtegin dynasty, succeeding his father even as a younger brother — backed by the powerful Queen Mother — contested his claim. Who is he?
Jalal al-Din Mangburni: Last shah of the Khwarazmian Empire from 1220 to 1231.
A protégé of Martin Luther King Jr., this Baptist minister and civil rights leader founded the organizations that merged into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition — who is he?
Jesse Jackson: American minister, activist and politician (1941–2026)
This English actor played the third incarnation of the Doctor on a beloved sci-fi series in the 1970s and later starred as a scarecrow brought to life in another family show — who is he?
This Polish statesman served as Chief of State after World War I and is regarded as the father of the Second Republic, re-established in 1918 after 123 years of partition. Who was he?

Named after a 1954 Ilya Ehrenburg novel, this mid-1950s-to-mid-1960s period saw Soviet censorship and repression relax following Stalin's death and the 'Secret Speech' denouncing him — what's it called?
Khrushchev thaw: Period of Soviet history, 1950s-60s.
Founded by Anton LaVey with the 1966 creation of the Church of Satan in San Francisco, this belief system blends humanism, hedonism, and showmanship, drawing on Nietzsche and Ayn Rand — what is it?
LaVeyan Satanism: Religious movement founded by Anton LaVey.
Revered as Quaid-e-Millat, "Leader of the Nation," this lawyer-statesman became his country's first prime minister in 1947 and was assassinated four years later. Who was he?
Liaquat Ali Khan: Prime Minister of Pakistan from 1947 to 1951.
This three-time French Prime Minister led the left-wing Popular Front government in the 1930s and later became a staunch opponent of the Vichy regime — who was he?
The first Filipino to lead a government over the entire Philippines, this president defeated Emilio Aguinaldo in the 1935 election and lent his name to a city in Metro Manila — who was he?
Manuel L. Quezon: President of the Philippines from 1935 to 1944.
The daughter of a former Pakistani prime minister, this politician made history in February 2024 as the first woman to become chief minister of Punjab — who is she?
Maryam Nawaz: Chief Minister of Punjab (born 1973)
He recovered Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261 and founded the dynasty that would rule the Byzantines until the city finally fell in 1453 — which emperor?
Michael VIII Palaiologos: Byzantine emperor from 1261 to 1282.
This Iranian prime minister's land reforms and social security programs ended abruptly in a 1953 coup engineered by the CIA and MI6 — who was he?
Mohammad Mosaddegh: Prime Minister of Iran from 1951 to 1953.
Serving as Israel's prime minister from 2021 to 2022, this politician and former special-forces soldier co-founded the tech company Cyota after growing up in Haifa — who is he?
Naftali Bennett: Prime Minister of Israel from 2021 to 2022. Bennett has served as the head of Bennett 2026 since 2025; the party is allied with Yesh Atid as part of an alliance called Together.
From 1965 to 1977 this Ukrainian-born official served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet — effectively the Soviet head of state. Who was he?

Announced by President Bush after the September 11 attacks, this was the official U.S. name for the first phase (2001-2014) of the Afghanistan war against al-Qaeda and the Taliban — what was it called?
Operation Enduring Freedom: Official name for the US's war on terror.
Known for championing charter schools, this former superintendent led school districts in Philadelphia and Chicago before running — and narrowly losing — a bid for Chicago mayor in 2023. Who is he?
Paul Vallas: American politician and school administrator (born 1953)
A protégé of the dictator Sulla, this Roman general and statesman celebrated three triumphs and was elected consul on three separate occasions during the late Republic — who was he?
Pompey: Roman general and statesman (106–48 BC)
In October 2021, this U.S. assistant secretary for health became the nation's first openly transgender four-star officer across all eight uniformed services — who is she?
Rachel Levine: American public health official (born 1957)

This short-lived 1990s state in the Balkans seceded from a disintegrating Yugoslavia in 1992, triggering a three-year war as rival Serb and Croat factions carved out their own unrecognized quasi-states — what state?
Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Balkan country (1992–1995)
Born in Tampico, Illinois, this future actor started as a sports broadcaster in Iowa in 1933 before moving to Hollywood and later serving as Screen Actors Guild president twice. Who was he?
Ronald Reagan: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989.
Nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005, this jurist became just the second Italian American justice on the Supreme Court, after Antonin Scalia — who is he?
Samuel Alito: US Supreme Court justice since 2006.

Once Adolf Hitler's personal chauffeur and bodyguard, this German officer rose to become the highest-ranking commissioned commander in the Waffen-SS despite having no formal staff training — who is he?
Sepp Dietrich: German Nazi politician and SS commander (1892–1966)

Lasting 872 days and killing an estimated 1.5 million from a prewar population of 3.2 million, this WWII blockade of the Soviet Union's second-largest city was never successfully captured — what was it?
Siege of Leningrad: Blockade by the Axis powers, 1941–1944.

Daughter of Darius III of Persia, she was captured after her father's defeat at Issus and became the second bride of the Macedonian conqueror at the Susa weddings in 324 BC, before being killed by his other spouse, Roxana — who was she?
Stateira (wife of Alexander the Great): Daughter of Darius III, died 323 BC.
A Thai Chinese general, he became the only king of Thonburi after leading the liberation of Siam from Burmese occupation and reuniting a country splintered among warlords — who was he?
Taksin: King of Siam from 1767 to 1782.

A protégé of Robert Walpole, this Whig statesman served as a Secretary of State for 30 unbroken years and dominated British foreign policy — and was twice Prime Minister. By which dukedom is he commonly known?
Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle: Prime Minister of Great Britain (1754–1756; 1757–1762)
This Indian politician served as Maharashtra's 19th chief minister from 2019 to 2022 while also editing a newspaper for over a decade — who is he?
Uddhav Thackeray: 19th Chief Minister of Maharashtra from 2019 to 2022 (born 1960)
In 1976, this Soviet pilot defected to the West by flying his MiG-25 'Foxbat' jet interceptor to Japan, handing the CIA what George H. W. Bush called an 'intelligence bonanza' — who is he?
Viktor Belenko: Soviet pilot who defected to the West (1947–2023)
One of the most popular presidents at his death in 1923, this Ohio newspaperman who built up the Marion Star saw his reputation later wrecked by exposed scandals — who was he?
Warren G. Harding: President of the United States from 1921 to 1923.
Raging from 1914 to 1918 and nicknamed 'the Great War,' this conflict's mass troop movements helped spread the deadly Spanish flu pandemic — which war?
World War I: 1914–1918 global conflict. The war saw important developments in weaponry including tanks, aircraft, artillery, machine guns, and chemical weapons.
This late-Qing statesman raised and organized the Xiang Army to crush the Taiping Rebellion and helped launch the Tongzhi Restoration — who was he?
Zeng Guofan: Chinese politician and military commander (1811–1872)

Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
Earth (formed ~4.54 billion years ago) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Joseph Henry is a physicist. Joseph Henry (December 17, 1797– May 13, 1878) was an American physicist and inventor who served as the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.
Pick the chemist from these four.
Primo Levi is a chemist. Primo Michele Levi (Italian: [ˈpriːmo ˈlɛːvi]; 31 July 1919 – 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.
What is the atomic number of Flerovium?
Flerovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fl and atomic number 114.
What is the atomic number of Yttrium?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.

Allergy is an exaggerated immune response where the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless allergen as a threat.

With atomic number 85 and symbol At, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, forming only as a decay product of heavier elements — name it?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.

Native to South American tropical forests, this thorny ornamental vine, bush, or tree produces large colorful bracts surrounding three small waxy flowers — what is this plant genus?

Originating from the now-discredited caloric theory of heat, this unit of energy is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius — name the unit?
Calorie is a unit of energy that originated from the caloric theory of heat.
This class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed body segments called proglottids into the environment to infect new hosts — what is this class called (scientific name)?

Released on a daily cycle and spiking when you're stressed, this glucocorticoid raises blood sugar through gluconeogenesis and even tamps down the immune system — what stress hormone is it?

Marked by a telltale skin rash plus progressive muscle weakness, this systemic autoimmune condition can also bring fever, weight loss and light sensitivity — which disease?
Dermatomyositis (DM) is a group of sytemic autoimmune inflammatory diseases primarily affecting the skin and skeletal muscles.

This American investor and podcaster coined the phrase 'intellectual dark web' and proposed a physics framework called 'Geometric Unity' — who is he?
Eric Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.

Found on every continent except Antarctica, this lizard lacks eyelids — instead its eyeballs are covered by a transparent membrane called a brille. What is it?
Gecko are small, mostly carnivorous lizards that have a wide distribution, found on every continent except Antarctica.
One of only two wild camelid species native to South America, this llama relative lives at lower elevations than its cousin, the vicuña — what is it called?
Guanaco (gwah-; Lama guanicoe) is a camelid native to South America, closely related to the domesticated llama.

Worldwide, too little dietary iodine is the leading cause of this endocrine condition, in which a sluggish thyroid leaves people cold-intolerant, exhausted, constipated, and prone to weight gain — what is it?
Hypothyroidism is an endocrine disease in which the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormones.
A Scottish surgeon who corrected clubfoot and squints, he's also dubbed by some the 'Father of Modern Hypnotism' — pioneering both hypnotic and chemical anaesthesia. Who was this gentleman scientist?
James Braid (surgeon) (19 June 1795 - 25 March 1860) was a Scottish surgeon, natural philosopher, and "gentleman scientist".
One species of this succulent plant genus, native mainly to Madagascar, became one of the first plants ever sent into space aboard a Soviet space station in 1979 — what genus is it?

Spread by the bite of sandflies and caused by a genus of protozoal parasites, this tropical disease can present as skin ulcers, disfiguring mucosal damage, or a more dangerous internal form. Name the disease?

This evergreen tree, native to the cooler hills of south-central China, is grown commercially for its orange fruit and is sometimes called the Japanese medlar. What is it?
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
Following fieldwork with the Omaha people and in Papua New Guinea and Bali, this anthropologist explored gender roles in her 1935 book Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies — who is she?
Margaret Mead (December 16, 1901 - November 15, 1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker, who appeared frequently in the mass media during the mid-twentieth century.
Despite little formal education, this self-made English scientist established the concept of the electromagnetic field and uncovered the principles behind electromagnetic induction — who is he?
Michael Faraday (22 September 1791 - 25 August 1867) was an English chemist and physicist who contributed vastly to the study of electrochemistry and electromagnetism.
This group of more than 30 rare neuromuscular disorders causes skeletal tissue to progressively weaken and break down, differing in which body parts are hit first and how fast — what's it called?

This raised region of tissue on the breast, surrounded by the darker-colored areola, is where milk exits the body through the lactiferous ducts during breastfeeding — name this body part?
Nipple is a raised region of tissue on the surface of the breast from which, in lactating females, milk from the mammary gland leaves the body through the lactiferous ducts to nurse an infant.
Usually caused by bacteria and sometimes requiring amputation in severe cases, this infectious inflammation of bone can be acute or chronic — which condition?

Recognized by a long beak and an enormous throat pouch used to drain water from scooped-up prey before swallowing, these large water birds come in eight living species worldwide — which birds?

What small, tailless, round-bodied mountain mammal — a close relative of the rabbit with short rounded ears — includes a large-eared Himalayan species that lives above 6,000 meters?

Lacking any real scientific definition, this British term for a large swimming crustacean has become almost interchangeable with 'shrimp' — what is it?
Prawn is a common name for small aquatic crustaceans with an exoskeleton and ten legs (members of the order of decapods), some of which are edible.
A zoonotic virus that triggers violent movements, a dread of water, and almost certain death once symptoms set in — usually one to three months after exposure. What is this disease?
Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that causes acute and severe encephalitis in humans and other mammals.
This British economist won the 1991 Nobel Memorial Prize and warned that the field was "suicidal" to become a hard science of choice while ignoring society, history, and culture — who was he?
Ronald Coase (29 December 1910 - 2 September 2013) was a British economist and author.

Which urban model uses digital technology and data from citizens, buildings, and cameras to improve sustainability, efficiency, and social inclusion?

Brainstem: Posterior part of the brain, adjoining and structurally continuous.
